replies.user: What is attention in a transformer?
replies.raw:
**Attention** lets each word in a sequence look at every other word and decide which ones matter most for understanding it.

Example: in "The bank by the river flooded," attention helps the model connect "bank" to "river" — not to money — by weighing those nearby words heavily.

What do you think happens when a model processes a word that could mean two different things?

replies.user: So each token looks back at the earlier tokens and decides which ones matter most?
replies.raw:
Close — but it's actually more than just looking *back*.

In the full attention mechanism, each token can attend to **every** token in the sequence, including ones that come after it (in some architectures).

What do you think might change if a model could *only* look backward versus in both directions?

replies.user: Explain more — go deeper on the same topic. Don't repeat what you already said.
replies.raw:
The key mechanism underneath: each token is turned into three vectors — a **Query**, a **Key**, and a **Value**.

Think of it like a library search. The Query is what you're looking for. Every other token has a Key (a label on the shelf) and a Value (the actual content).

The model computes a score by matching your Query against every Key, then uses those scores to take a weighted blend of all the Values.

That weighted blend is what the token "learns" from its context in this layer.

Two failure modes worth knowing:

- **Long sequences** are expensive: scoring every token against every other token scales as n², so a 10,000-token document is vastly more costly than a 1,000-token one.
- **Uniform attention** (every score roughly equal) means the token learned nothing useful — it just averaged everything, which is nearly as bad as ignoring context entirely.

One thing that surprises most people: the model doesn't learn *which* tokens to attend to directly. It learns the Q, K, and V weight matrices during training, and the attention pattern *emerges* from those weights meeting the actual input.

So here's the sharper question: if attention patterns emerge rather than being programmed, what does that imply about our ability to *explain* why a model made a specific prediction?

It reads **numbers** — and the journey from your sentence to those numbers is where everything begins.

[KEY]Tokenization converts your text into a sequence of number IDs before the model ever "sees" it.[/KEY]

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens, each mapped to a unique number. So "cat" might become token ID 123 (made-up ID for illustration), and "cats" might be a completely different number.[/EX]

[Q]
What does a language model actually receive as its input — what form is your prompt in when the model first processes it?
A) The original words, exactly as you typed them
B) A sequence of numbers representing word-chunks
C) A compressed audio recording of the text
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A sequence of numbers representing word-chunks
replies.raw:
Exactly right — the model never sees raw text, only those number sequences.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Those numbers get transformed into something richer: points in a massive mathematical space called an **embedding space**.

Words with similar meanings end up *near each other* in this space — "king" and "queen" are closer to each other than either is to "bicycle." But here's the problem that creates: the word "bank" gets the same starting point whether you mean a riverbank or a financial institution.

[KEY]Attention is the mechanism that lets the model adjust each word's meaning based on the other words around it.[/KEY]

[EX]In "I sat on the bank of the river," the model's attention mechanism notices "river" nearby and shifts "bank" toward the riverbank meaning. In "I put cash in the bank," attention to "cash" pulls it the other way. A standalone "I went to the bank" stays genuinely ambiguous — the surrounding words don't decide it.[/EX]

[Q]
Why can't the model just look up "bank" in a dictionary to figure out which meaning to use?
A) Dictionaries don't have enough definitions
B) The model has no internet access during processing
C) Meaning depends on surrounding context, not the word alone
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked A) Dictionaries don't have enough definitions
replies.raw:
Actually, C is the one here — even a perfect dictionary listing every meaning of "bank" wouldn't help, because the dictionary can't tell you *which* meaning fits *this* sentence. That requires looking at the words around it.

Think of it this way: a dictionary gives you a menu of options. Attention is what *orders from the menu* based on context.

Now for the payoff — what the model actually *does* with all of this.

After attention has shaped each token's meaning using its neighbors, the model makes a prediction: **what token should come next?**

It does this one token at a time, every single time, for every word in its reply.

[KEY]An LLM generates text by repeatedly predicting the single most likely next token, given everything that came before.[/KEY]

[EX]Feed the model "The cat sat on the ___" and it assigns probabilities to every token in its vocabulary. "Mat," "floor," and "couch" score high. "Democracy" scores near zero. The model picks from the high-probability options — and then does it again for the token after that.[/EX]
